items.stem: A maximum price set below the equilibrium price will cause
items.answer: a shortage (excess demand)
items.markingKey: Price ceiling below equilibrium → Qd > Qs.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a diagram, the effect of a maximum price set below the equilibrium price.
items.answer: At the lower price quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls, causing a shortage (Qd − Qs). Goods must be rationed by queuing or other means, and a black market may develop at higher prices.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: below equilibrium; 1 mark: shortage; 1 mark: consequence [3]

items.stem: Explain why a minimum price for an agricultural product may lead to government spending.
items.answer: At the minimum price above equilibrium there is a surplus; to maintain the price the government must buy the surplus, which costs money and storage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: surplus; 1 mark: government buys surplus [2]

items.stem: In the market for textbooks, Qd = 170 − 5P and Qs = 70 + 5P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government introduces a maximum price of $9. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity without intervention. (b) Calculate quantity demanded and supplied at the controlled price and the resulting shortage. (c) Explain one way in which the shortage may be allocated and one likely consequence.
items.answer: (a) $10, 120 thousand. (b) Qd = 125, Qs = 115: shortage of 10 thousand. (c) Queuing, waiting lists or rationing; black market at higher prices.

items.stem: In the market for smartphones, Qd = 115 − 5P and Qs = −35 + 5P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government introduces a minimum price of $16. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity without intervention. (b) Calculate quantity demanded and supplied at the controlled price and the resulting surplus. (c) If the government buys the surplus, calculate the cost.
items.answer: (a) $15, 40 thousand. (b) Qd = 35, Qs = 45: surplus of 10 thousand. (c) 10,000 × $16 = $160,000.

items.stem: In the market for fresh fruit, Qd = 250 − 10P and Qs = 25 + 5P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government introduces a minimum price of $18. (a) Calculate the equilibrium price and quantity without intervention. (b) Calculate quantity demanded and supplied at the controlled price and the resulting surplus. (c) If the government buys the surplus, calculate the cost.
items.answer: (a) $15, 100 thousand. (b) Qd = 70, Qs = 115: surplus of 45 thousand. (c) 45,000 × $18 = $810,000.

The proposed tax is $2 per unit. Some ministers prefer a ban on advertising or a public information campaign instead. (a) Calculate the weekly tax revenue. (b) Explain how the incidence of the tax is shared between consumers and producers.
items.answer: (a) $112,500 (b) Consumers pay $0.75 more per unit; producers receive $1.25 less; depends on relative elasticities.

items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $12, 50 [2] (b) Credit: $13, 46 [2] (c) 3 × 46 thousand [1]

items.stem: Bogotá introduces rent controls that keep rents well below the market level. Explain why the number of flats for rent may fall over time.
items.answer: Lower returns reduce landlords’ incentive to rent out or maintain flats; supply contracts, so shortages grow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower incentive; 1 mark: supply falls [2]

items.stem: What is a specific tax?
options: A tax paid only by consumers
A tax that is a percentage of the price
A fixed amount of tax per unit sold
items.answer: A fixed amount of tax per unit sold
items.markingKey: Shifts supply up in parallel by the tax.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a specific tax and an ad valorem tax.
items.answer: A specific tax is a fixed amount per unit (parallel upward shift of supply); an ad valorem tax is a percentage of price, so the tax per unit rises with price (supply curve pivots and diverges).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why the incidence of an indirect tax depends on the price elasticity of demand.
items.answer: If demand is inelastic, producers can pass most of the tax on as a higher price without losing many sales, so consumers bear most; if elastic, producers absorb more.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inelastic → consumers; 1 mark: elastic → producers [2]

items.stem: In the market for rice, Qd = 64 − 3P and Qs = 16 + 3P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government imposes a specific tax of $1 per unit. Calculate the new price paid by consumers.
items.markingKey: Supply becomes Qs = 16 + 3(P − 1); 64 − 3P = 13 + 3P → P = 8.5.

items.stem: In the market for restaurant meals, Qd = 230 − 4P and Qs = 70 + 4P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government imposes a specific tax of $1 per unit. (a) Calculate the equilibrium before the tax and the new price paid by consumers, price received by producers and quantity. (b) Calculate the tax revenue and the share of the tax paid by consumers. (c) Explain why consumers bear this share.
items.answer: (a) Before: $20, 150. After: consumers pay $20.50, producers receive $19.50, Q = 148. (b) Revenue = 1 × 148 thousand = $148,000; consumers bear 50% (consumer burden $74,000, producer burden $74,000). (c) Demand and supply are equally responsive, so the burden is shared equally.
items.markingKey: (a) original equilibrium [1]; new prices and quantity [2] (b) revenue [1]; consumer share 0.5/1 [1] (c) relative elasticities [1] [6]

items.stem: In the market for restaurant meals, Qd = 160 − 4P and Qs = −40 + 4P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government imposes a specific tax of $3 per unit. (c) Explain why consumers bear this share.
items.answer: (a) Before: $25, 60. After: consumers pay $26.50, producers receive $23.50, Q = 54. (b) Revenue = 3 × 54 thousand = $162,000; consumers bear 50% (consumer burden $81,000, producer burden $81,000). (c) Demand and supply are equally responsive, so the burden is shared equally.
items.markingKey: (a) original equilibrium [1]; new prices and quantity [2] (b) revenue [1]; consumer share 1.5/3 [1] (c) relative elasticities [1] [6]

items.stem: What is the effect of a subsidy to producers on the supply curve?
options: It shifts the supply curve downwards (to the right) by the amount of the subsidy
It shifts demand to the right
It shifts supply to the left
items.answer: It shifts the supply curve downwards (to the right) by the amount of the subsidy
items.markingKey: Lower costs.

items.stem: Explain how a subsidy affects the price and quantity in a market.
items.answer: A subsidy lowers producers’ costs, shifting supply right/down; price paid by consumers falls and quantity rises; producers receive the market price plus the subsidy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: supply shift; 1 mark: lower price/higher quantity [2]

items.stem: Explain two possible problems of using subsidies to encourage consumption of merit goods.
items.answer: Opportunity cost/tax burden; firms may become inefficient or dependent; difficult to set the right amount; benefit may go to producers rather than consumers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each problem explained [4]

items.stem: In the market for textiles, Qd = 64 − 4P and Qs = 16 + 4P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government gives producers a subsidy of $2 per unit. Calculate the new price paid by consumers.

In the market for bottled water, Qd = 180 − 4P and Qs = −20 + 6P (Q in thousands, P in dollars). The government gives producers a subsidy of $3 per unit. (a) Calculate the new price paid by consumers, the price received by producers and the new quantity. (b) Calculate the total cost of the subsidy to the government. (c) Calculate the share of the subsidy received by consumers and comment.
items.answer: (a) Consumers $18.20, producers $21.20, Q = 107.2 thousand. (b) 3 × 107.2 thousand = $321,600. (c) Consumers gain $1.80 per unit (60% of the subsidy): consumers gain most, demand relatively inelastic.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [1] (c) share and comment [2] [5]

items.stem: Which is an example of direct provision by the government?
options: State-run schools that charge no fees
items.answer: State-run schools that charge no fees
items.markingKey: Government produces/supplies the good.

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using regulation to reduce pollution.
items.answer: Advantage: clear, enforceable limits with certain outcomes. Disadvantage: costly to monitor; no incentive to cut below the limit; may be set at the wrong level; firms may relocate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: advantage; 1 mark: disadvantage [2]

items.stem: Explain why a government might choose to provide healthcare directly rather than subsidise private providers.
items.answer: Ensures universal access regardless of ability to pay, controls quality and coverage; avoids profit-driven under-provision in poor areas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: equity/access; 1 mark: control [2]

items.stem: The health ministry of Quentara runs a TV campaign on the dangers of drink-driving. Which method of government intervention is used?
items.answer: Provision of information
items.markingKey: Provision of information: improves knowledge of harms.

items.stem: Westaria bans smoking in all restaurants and offices. Which method of government intervention is used? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Rules and regulations: a legal restriction on behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Rules and regulations; 1 mark: explanation – a legal restriction on behaviour. [2]

What is meant by an unintended consequence of government intervention?
options: An outcome of a policy that was not planned or expected
A tax that raises more revenue than planned
A policy that is never implemented
The intended result of a policy
items.answer: An outcome of a policy that was not planned or expected
items.markingKey: Side effects that may worsen allocation.

items.stem: Which is an unintended consequence of a high tax on cigarettes?
items.answer: Increased smuggling and illegal sales
items.markingKey: Black markets.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why government intervention may lead to unintended consequences.
items.answer: Imperfect information about costs/benefits; people change behaviour (evasion, substitution, black markets); administrative costs; political pressures; time lags.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason explained [4]

items.stem: Rent controls in Karachi led landlords to sell their flats rather than let them, reducing the supply of rental housing. Which unintended consequence is shown?
items.answer: Reduced supply/shortage
items.markingKey: Reduced supply/shortage: lower returns cut the incentive to supply.

items.stem: During a class discussion Elena said: ‘A minimum price creates a shortage because the price is higher.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A binding minimum price (above equilibrium) creates excess supply: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A binding minimum price (above equilibrium) creates excess supply: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. [2]

options: A tax calculated as a percentage of the price
items.answer: A tax calculated as a percentage of the price

items.stem: Explain why a tax on fresh fruit might raise little revenue if demand is very price elastic.
items.answer: Consumers switch away when the price rises, so the quantity sold (tax base) falls sharply.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: elastic demand; 1 mark: small tax base [2]

items.stem: A sales tax of 15% is charged on school backpacks in Merania. The price before tax is $40. Calculate the price including tax.

items.answer: (a) Tax $4; price $84. (b) $4.80 (c) The tax per unit is a percentage of price, so it is larger at higher prices; the vertical distance between the supply curves increases with price.

items.stem: The government of Fendaria builds and runs free public libraries. Which method of government intervention is used?
items.answer: Direct provision
items.markingKey: Direct provision: the state supplies the good itself, financed by taxes.

items.stem: The government of Ostrelia pays firms a subsidy for each worker they train. Explain one possible unintended consequence.
items.answer: Firms may claim for training they would have done anyway (deadweight), or provide low-quality training to collect the subsidy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: consequence; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: A ban on single-use plastic bags in Lima increased the use of thicker bags made from more plastic. Which unintended consequence is shown?
items.answer: Substitution into other harmful goods
items.markingKey: Substitution into other harmful goods: consumers switched to alternatives with their own problems.

items.stem: Extract: The government of Ostrelia plans to tax cinema tickets to reduce consumption. Economists estimate the market as Qd = 135 − 5P and Qs = −15 + 5P (Q in thousands per week, P in dollars). The proposed tax is $2 per unit. Some ministers prefer a ban on advertising or a public information campaign instead. (a) Calculate the new price paid by consumers and the new quantity. (b) Explain how the incidence of the tax is shared between consumers and producers.
items.answer: (a) $16, 55 (b) Consumers pay $1 more per unit; producers receive $1 less; depends on relative elasticities.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: $16, 55 [2] (b) Credit: Consumers pay $1 more per unit; producers receive $1 less; depends on relative elasticities. [3]
